name: Coordinate Transformations
text:
# Coordinate Transformations
## Overview
Coordinate transformations are deterministic functions $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i : \mathbb{R}^D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{F_i}$ that map input spatial coordinates to a transformed domain before evaluation by factor fields [S1, unofficial]. They solve the problem of defining the geometric relationship between the input space and the basis functions or feature grids, enabling the reuse of basis patterns across different locations and scales [S1, unofficial]. What sets them apart from sibling methods is their role as a pre-processing step within the [Factor Fields framework](#19669-factor-fields-framework.md); unlike [Homogeneous Coordinate Transformation](21412-homogeneous-coordinate-transformation.md) which handles camera-to-world projection, coordinate transformations here handle the internal mapping for neural representation factors, such as positional encoding or hash lookups [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
Coordinate transformations are defined as deterministic functions $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i$ that operate on input coordinates $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^D$ to produce transformed coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^{F_i}$ [S1, unofficial]. The dimensionality of the output space $F_i$ does not need to match the input dimensionality $D$, allowing the domain of the subsequent basis functions to change accordingly [S1, unofficial]. Transformations are categorized into two types based on their spatial properties: periodic transformations, which allow the same basis function to be applied at multiple spatial locations and optionally at multiple different scales while varying the coefficients, and non-periodic transformations, which do not exhibit periodicity [S1, unofficial]. The identity transformation is a specific case defined as $\gamma(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$, where the input coordinates are passed unchanged [S1, unofficial]. In the Factor Fields framework, the output of a coordinate transformation $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i(\mathbf{x})$ is passed to a factor field $f_i$ [S1, unofficial]. The parameters of the factor fields are optimized, while the coordinate transformations are considered deterministic functions [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Positional Encoding
A periodic transformation used in [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md), treating the MLP network as a factor with positional encoding transformation [S1, unofficial].

### Hash Transformation
A transformation used in Instant-NGP, treating the tabular encoding as a factor with hash transformation [S1, unofficial].

### Axis-aligned Orthogonal Projections
Transformations used in TensoRF, involving 2D and 1D projections for tensor factorization-based representations [S1, unofficial]. These are limited to orthogonal transformations and decompose the signal into Vector-Matrix or CANDECOMP-PARAFAC factors [S1, unofficial].

### Identity Transformation
Defined as $\gamma(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$, used for coefficient fields in DiF and for feature grids in DVGO/Plenoxels [S1, unofficial].

### Periodic Basis Transformation
Used in [Dictionary Field](#11944-dictionary-fields.md) (DiF) for the basis function factor, allowing the same basis to be applied at multiple spatial locations and scales [S1, unofficial]. This enables efficient representation of global and local signal properties [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of coordinate transformations in this context was formalized within the Factor Fields framework, introduced in "Factor Fields: A Unified Framework for Neural Fields and Beyond" [S1, unofficial]. This framework generalizes previous neural representations by treating them as factors with specific domain transformations [S1, unofficial]. Prior to this, methods like NeRF used positional encoding [S1, unofficial], Instant-NGP used hash transformations [S1, unofficial], and DVGO/Plenoxels used identity transformations for feature grids [S1, unofficial]. TensoRF introduced axis-aligned orthogonal projections for tensor factorization [S1, unofficial]. The Factor Fields framework unified these approaches, demonstrating that many single-factor representations could be seen as using either a basis function (like NeRF and Instant-NGP) or a coefficient function (like DVGO and Plenoxels) [S1, unofficial]. The framework allows for flexible combinations of these factors and transformations, leading to novel representation designs like DiF [S1, unofficial].

## Sources
[S1] Factor Fields: A Unified Framework for Neural Fields and Beyond, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.01226, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
